title: Indian Scientists Build Light-Controlled Nanobots That Hunt Breast Cancer Cells
excerpt: Researchers at INST Mohali and BARC Mumbai created fuel-free nanobots that move toward tumors using near-infrared light, combining two cancer-killing mechanisms in a single platform
body:
• Researchers at the Institute of Nano Science and Technology (INST), Mohali, developed nanobots that use near-infrared light to navigate toward breast cancer cells and destroy them.
  • The nanobots combine photothermal and photodynamic therapy — generating heat and reactive oxygen species simultaneously — for more effective tumor killing than either method alone.
  • Folic acid on the nanobot surface lets them selectively bind to breast cancer cells while sparing healthy tissue, with treatment intensity controlled externally by laser.
  • The system was tested successfully in both lab-grown cancer cells and tumor-bearing mice, with results published in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces.

A team of Indian researchers has developed a light-powered nanobot that can actively seek out breast cancer cells and destroy them using two simultaneous attack mechanisms — a development that could eventually make cancer treatment far more precise and less damaging than conventional chemotherapy.

The study, published in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces, was led by Dr. Jiban Jyoti Panda at INST Mohali in collaboration with Dr. Santosh K. Gupta of the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) in Mumbai. Swapnil Srivastava served as first author, with Annu Balhara, Pankaj Kharra, and Jyoti Yadav rounding out the research team.

How the Nanobots Work

The scientists engineered the nanobots from upconversion nanoparticles coated with polydopamine, a biocompatible polymer. When hit with a 980-nanometer near-infrared (NIR) laser, the polydopamine coating generates localized heat, creating a temperature gradient that propels the nanobots toward the light source — a phenomenon called phototaxis.

Unlike many existing nanomedicine systems that rely on passive delivery — essentially hoping nanoparticles drift to the right location after injection — these nanobots are fuel-free and externally steered. Researchers can direct them toward a tumor by positioning the laser, giving clinicians a degree of control that passive systems lack.

"India estimated 1.56 million new cancer cases across all types in 2024, per an ICMR report, with breast cancer incidence rising at approximately 1.83 percent per year."

The same NIR exposure activates a second weapon. A photosensitizer attached to the nanobots generates reactive oxygen species (ROS), highly reactive molecules that damage and kill cancer cells. The combination of heat-based killing (photothermal therapy) and ROS-based killing (photodynamic therapy) proved more effective than either approach alone in the team's testing.

Targeting Cancer, Sparing Healthy Tissue

To improve targeting accuracy, the researchers coated the nanobots with folic acid. Many breast cancer cells overexpress folate receptors on their surface, so the folic acid acts as a homing signal — the nanobots preferentially bind to cancer cells rather than healthy ones.

The treatment intensity can also be dialed up or down externally. Factors including laser intensity, local pH, and glutathione concentration all regulate the nanobots' therapeutic output. And because the system uses near-infrared light rather than ultraviolet or visible light, it penetrates deeper into tissue with less risk of collateral damage to surrounding cells.

Why It Matters

Breast cancer is the most common cancer among Indian women, with national mortality tripling from roughly 33,000 deaths in 1991 to over 101,000 in 2023, according to Global Burden of Disease data. India estimated 1.56 million new cancer cases across all types in 2024, per an ICMR report, with breast cancer incidence rising at approximately 1.83 percent per year.

Conventional chemotherapy remains the backbone of treatment but carries well-documented drawbacks: drugs circulate systemically, damaging healthy tissue alongside cancerous cells and causing side effects ranging from nausea to organ damage. Many tumors also develop drug resistance over time, reducing treatment effectiveness.

A targeted system that can be guided to tumors externally and activated on demand addresses both problems. The dual-therapy approach also reduces the odds of resistance, since cancer cells must survive two distinct killing mechanisms simultaneously.

The Research Team

The work comes from INST Mohali, an autonomous institute under India's Department of Science and Technology, which has built a track record in nanomedicine research. Dr. Panda's lab has previously worked on nano-based approaches to cataract treatment, tumor management, and drug delivery systems. The collaboration with BARC Mumbai — India's premier nuclear and atomic research facility — brought expertise in the upconversion nanoparticle chemistry at the core of the nanobot design.

What Comes Next

The researchers demonstrated the nanobots' effectiveness in both laboratory-grown cancer cells and breast tumor-bearing mice, showing stronger tumor inhibition with the combined photothermal-photodynamic approach compared to either therapy alone. The nanobots' active movement toward target areas was confirmed in animal models.

However, the technology remains in the preclinical stage. Further studies will be needed to assess long-term safety, optimize dosing, and determine whether the results translate to more complex tumor environments before any path to clinical trials in humans opens up. The researchers noted that the multifunctional platform could become an important step toward precision cancer therapy — but acknowledged significant work remains between a successful mouse study and a viable human treatment.
